For equilibrium the sum of moments about the pivot is zero, so $W$ times its $1.0\text{ m}$ arm must equal $50\text{ N}$ times its arm on the Q side.
Calculate how far the beam centre is to the right of the pivot and then solve $W \times 1.0\text{ m} = 50\text{ N} \times \text{that distance}$.
walkthrough: Take moments about the pivot because the unknown pivot force then has zero moment. The beam is uniform, so its $50\text{ N}$ weight acts at its midpoint, $1.5\text{ m}$ from P.

Distance of beam weight from pivot: the pivot is $1.0\text{ m}$ from P, so the midpoint is $1.5 - 1.0 = 0.5\text{ m}$ to the right of the pivot. Distance of $W$ from pivot is $1.0\text{ m}$ to the left.

$W$ tends to turn the beam anticlockwise about the pivot and the beam weight tends to turn it clockwise, so for equilibrium the magnitudes are equal: $\text{sum of clockwise moments} = \text{sum of anticlockwise moments}$.
Substitute with units: $W \times 1.0\text{ m} = 50\text{ N} \times 0.5\text{ m}$.
Solve: $W = 25\text{ N}$ with unit $\text{N}$, which matches the clockwise-anticlockwise balance. This is option A.
